client: I've been really struggling this past week with this big presentation I have coming up at our annual conference, and honestly, I'm kind of a mess about it. Yesterday during practice I completely blanked — like, my mind just went totally empty in front of my colleagues, and now I can't stop replaying that moment over and over. I'm not sure talking about it is really going to fix anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when you're not sure it will help, and I'm really glad you did. That moment of blanking in front of your colleagues sounds genuinely distressing, and it makes complete sense that your mind keeps returning to it — our brains have a way of replaying painful moments as if trying to "solve" them. I'm curious, when that memory replays, what's the thought that tends to follow it — what does that moment *mean* to you about yourself or how the presentation will go?

client: Honestly, when that moment replays, the thought that hits me hardest is that I'm going to completely fall apart at the actual conference and everyone's going to see that I don't really know what I'm talking about. Like, it feels like proof that I'm a fraud — that I've somehow been faking competence this whole time and now it's all about to unravel in front of everyone. And the worst part is, I can't shake the feeling that this time, it's actually true.
therapist: That feeling of being "found out" is incredibly painful, and I want you to know it's also one of the most common experiences among capable, hardworking people — it even has a name, impostor syndrome. But I'd gently invite you to pause on the word "proof" — one moment of blanking during a practice run is one data point, and I'm wondering what other evidence exists about your competence that we might be overlooking. Can you think of a time, maybe recently, where your knowledge or skills genuinely showed up in a way that others recognized?

client: I mean, yeah, my manager did pull me aside after a team meeting last month and said I handled a really tough Q&A session better than anyone expected. And I guess there have been other moments like that, but the thing is, when I'm in that replay loop, those memories just don't feel as real or as heavy as the blanking moment did. It's like the bad stuff has this louder volume, and I'm not sure just reminding myself of the good stuff is actually going to quiet it down.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — your brain isn't being objective, it's turning up the volume on the threatening memory while quietly muting the evidence that contradicts it, which is a very human but very misleading mental habit we call the negativity bias. And you're right that simply *reminding* yourself of good moments often isn't enough, because it can feel like you're just arguing with the fear rather than truly updating it. I'm wondering — when your manager gave you that feedback after the Q&A, what was it like in your body in that moment, and do you think you actually let yourself take it in?

client: Honestly, in that moment I remember feeling kind of relieved but also almost suspicious of it, like I was waiting for the "but" that never came. I think I smiled and said thank you, but inside I was already kind of dismissing it, telling myself he was probably just being nice or trying to keep morale up. So no, I don't think I really let it land — and that's a weird thing to realize, because I'm not sure I even know how to let something good actually sink in.
therapist: That's a genuinely profound realization — you've essentially built a one-way filter where criticism and failure get absorbed deeply, while praise and success get screened out before they can even reach you. It's like your mind has been collecting evidence for the "fraud" story while quietly rejecting anything that challenges it, which means the verdict was never really fair. I'm curious — what do you think it would actually take, in that moment when your manager praised you, for you to let yourself be someone who *deserved* to hear it?

client: That question actually kind of stops me, because I genuinely don't know what it would take — and that's unsettling to sit with. Part of me thinks I'd need like, overwhelming, undeniable evidence before I'd let myself believe it, but then I also wonder if even that wouldn't be enough, because I'd probably find a way to explain it away. It's like the bar keeps moving, and I'm not sure I'm the one setting it anymore.
therapist: What you just described — a bar that keeps moving no matter how well you do — is such an honest and courageous thing to notice, because it reveals that the problem isn't actually a lack of evidence, it's that a part of you has decided the verdict in advance. That's not a character flaw; it's a protective pattern that probably made sense at some point in your life, even if it's working against you now. I'm wondering, does any part of you recognize where that voice came from — was there a time or a place where it first felt necessary to stay suspicious of your own success?

client: That question hits somewhere deeper than I expected, and I find myself thinking about my dad, who was never really someone who celebrated anything — like, doing well was just what you were supposed to do, so there was never any acknowledgment, just a raised bar. I think I learned pretty early that feeling good about yourself was almost dangerous, like it would make you sloppy or set you up to be embarrassed later. I'm not sure I've ever connected that to the presentation stuff before, but saying it out loud right now feels kind of significant and also a little overwhelming.
therapist: What you just connected is really significant — you essentially learned from someone you loved and depended on that self-acknowledgment was a liability, and so you internalized his voice to protect yourself, not realizing it would follow you into every conference room and practice session. It makes so much sense that this feels both meaningful and overwhelming right now, and I want you to know there's no pressure to untangle all of it today. I'm curious — now that you can see that voice as something you *learned* rather than something that's simply *true*, does it feel even slightly different to you?

client: It does feel slightly different, yeah — like there's a tiny bit of distance between me and that voice that wasn't there before, which is strange because I've lived with it so long it just felt like my own thinking. But I also want to be honest that I'm a little worried this is one of those things that makes sense in a therapy session and then just evaporates the moment I'm standing at that podium feeling my heart race. Like, how do I actually hold onto this when the fear kicks in and my body is doing its own thing?
therapist: That tiny bit of distance you're feeling right now is actually really important — it's not just an insight, it's a skill you can practice strengthening, so that gap between you and the voice gets wider over time rather than evaporating. You're absolutely right that insight alone won't calm a racing heart in the moment, which is why we'd want to pair this awareness with something concrete and physical you can anchor to when your body starts to panic. So I'm wondering — in the past, when you've felt overwhelmed and then somehow steadied yourself, what did that look like, even in small ways?

client: I guess there have been moments — like sometimes before a difficult conversation I'll just stop and take a few slow breaths, and it does take the edge off a little, even if I always feel kind of silly doing it. But I'm not sure that's going to be enough when I'm standing at a podium in front of a hundred people and my mind goes blank like it did in practice, because that felt like a completely different level of panic. I worry that whatever small thing works in a quiet moment just won't be accessible when everything's actually on the line.
therapist: You already have a tool that works — and the fact that you dismiss it as "silly" is actually that same inherited voice telling you that something simple and self-caring couldn't possibly be enough for someone like you. What's interesting is that the breathing doesn't need to *eliminate* the panic to be useful; it just needs to buy you a second of space, which is exactly that same tiny distance you found today between you and your father's voice. I'm wondering if between now and your presentation, you'd be open to a small experiment — practicing those breaths *specifically* in higher-pressure moments, not to feel silly or calm, but just to see if that gap shows up even a little when the stakes feel real?

client: I hear what you're saying, and that reframe about the "silly" feeling being the same voice actually landed in a way I didn't expect. But I guess my hesitation is that practicing in smaller high-pressure moments feels manageable in theory, and then the conference is just so much bigger — like, I'm worried I'll practice and it'll work a few times and then I'll convince myself I'm ready, and the blanking will happen anyway and it'll feel even worse because I thought I had a handle on it. I'm willing to try it, but I want to be honest that part of me is already bracing for it to not be enough.
therapist: The part of you that's already bracing for failure before you've even tried is worth noticing — it's that same protective voice trying to soften a blow that hasn't happened yet, which is a very human thing to do but also a way of living in a future that isn't real. And I want to gently offer this: even if you practice, and you still blank at the podium, that wouldn't mean the work was wasted — it would mean you're someone who blanked *and* had more tools than before, which is genuinely different from where you started. I'm curious — what would it mean for you to go into that conference not with a guarantee that it goes perfectly, but with a slightly kinder response ready for yourself if it doesn't?

client: That question is harder than it sounds, because honestly I'm not sure I know what a kinder response to myself would even look like — like, I can imagine saying the words "it's okay, you tried," but I don't know if I'd actually mean them or if it would just feel hollow. I think part of me believes that if I go in with a backup plan for failure, I'm somehow already giving up, even though I can hear how irrational that sounds when I say it out loud. But I guess what it might mean is... going in knowing that one bad moment doesn't have to be the whole verdict, and maybe that's a version of kindness I could at least start to try on.
therapist: What you just arrived at on your own — "one bad moment doesn't have to be the whole verdict" — is genuinely powerful, and I want you to notice that you found that yourself, which matters. And you're right that self-compassion can feel hollow at first, like wearing clothes that don't quite fit yet, but that's not because it's false — it's because it's unfamiliar, and unfamiliar things take practice just like the breathing does. I'm wondering if you could hold that phrase — "one moment isn't the whole verdict" — not as something you fully believe yet, but as something you're willing to try on and see how it fits as the conference gets closer?
